common_name: Red Spy Apple (Red-Skinned Northern Spy Sport, Cornell Breeding Parent)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer nearby.

directions: Red Spy is a deeper-colored, more evenly blushed bud sport of the classic New York heirloom Northern Spy, selected for improved red skin coloring while retaining the parent's very large fruit size, crisp dense flesh, and exceptionally long storage life. Cornell breeders at the Geneva research station used it as a parent alongside Golden Delicious to produce Spigold, passing on its size and firm texture to that cross. The tree shares Northern Spy's slow-to-bear habit and long lifespan, so plan for a multi-year wait before significant production begins. Thin fruit in years of heavy set to reduce biennial bearing and support fruit size on this large-fruited strain.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — apple breeding archives
New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva
Orange Pippin Fruit Trees — Northern Spy sport records

common_name: Clivia Apple (German Breeding Parent of Pinova)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer nearby.

directions: Clivia was bred at the Institute for Fruit Research in Dresden-Pillnitz, Germany, from a cross involving Golden Delicious and the cold-hardy Duchess of Oldenburg, combining a measure of Oldenburg's hardiness with Golden Delicious-style sweetness. It is grown today chiefly as a historical curiosity and breeding parent rather than a widely marketed dessert apple, most notably contributing to the German cultivar Pinova when crossed again with Golden Delicious. The medium, red-flushed fruit over a green-yellow ground color has crisp, juicy, mildly aromatic flesh good for fresh eating. The tree is moderately vigorous and reasonably disease-tolerant for a mid-20th-century German release, making it an interesting addition for collectors tracing the parentage of modern club apples.
sources: Julius Kühn-Institut (Dresden-Pillnitz) fruit breeding records
Orange Pippin Fruit Trees — Pinova parentage notes
National Fruit Collection, Brogdale (UK) — Clivia accession records

common_name: Lady Williams Apple (Late-Ripening Western Australian Parent of Pink Lady)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; benefits from a long, warm autumn to fully mature its very late fruit.

directions: Lady Williams was discovered as a chance seedling near Donnybrook, Western Australia in the 1930s by orchardist A.G. Williams, and is remarkable for ripening later than almost any other apple, often hanging on the tree into early winter in its home climate. John Cripps used it as the pollen parent, crossed onto Golden Delicious, to breed both Cripps Pink (Pink Lady) and Sundowner, passing on its deep red color, dense storage-friendly flesh, and unusually low chill requirement for a full-sized apple. The fruit itself is small to medium, very firm, and tart when picked, mellowing into a crisp, tangy apple useful for fresh eating and cooking after some storage. Its low chill requirement and heat tolerance during the long finishing period make it one of the few apples that can be grown to full maturity in mild-winter, warm-autumn climates.
sources: Western Australian Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development — apple breeding history
Orange Pippin Fruit Trees — Lady Williams variety notes
Department of Agriculture and Food, Western Australia — Cripps Pink development records

common_name: Ingrid Marie Apple (Danish Heirloom Parent of Elstar)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer nearby.

directions: Ingrid Marie was discovered in Denmark around 1910, likely a seedling connected to Cox's Orange Pippin, and became a widely grown dessert apple across Scandinavia and northern Europe for its rich, aromatic flavor and attractive deep red-flushed skin over a yellow-green background. Dutch breeders crossed it with Golden Delicious to produce Elstar, passing along its crisp texture and complex, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor to that now-common commercial variety. The fruit stores respectably for a mid-season apple and is well suited to fresh eating, with dense, juicy flesh that holds its character for several weeks after harvest. The tree is a reliable, moderately vigorous bearer well adapted to the cool, maritime climates of its native range.
sources: Orange Pippin Fruit Trees — Elstar parentage and Ingrid Marie notes
National Fruit Collection, Brogdale (UK) — Ingrid Marie accession records
Pometum, Royal Veterinary and Agricultural University of Denmark — historic Danish apple documentation

common_name: Hedelfingen Cherry (Hedelfinger Riesenkirsche, German Heirloom Sweet Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; requires a compatible pollinizer cultivar planted nearby.

directions: Hedelfingen, known fully in Germany as Hedelfinger Riesenkirsche, is a 19th-century heirloom sweet cherry from the village of Hedelfingen near Stuttgart, bearing large, dark mahogany-red to near-black, heart-shaped fruit with rich, sweet flavor. It is self-unfruitful but blooms in the mid-to-late window that overlaps with many other sweet cherry cultivars, which has made it a long-standing standard pollinizer choice in commercial and heirloom orchards alike, including for late-season cultivars such as Regina. The fruit has moderate resistance to cracking compared with older, softer-fleshed heirlooms, though it is less crack-tolerant than modern firm-fleshed releases. Net trees against birds as fruit colors, and provide deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through fruit development to reduce splitting.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit — sweet cherry pollination compatibility charts
Orange Pippin Fruit Trees — Hedelfingen variety notes
University of California Fruit and Nut Research and Information Center — cherry cultivar records

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun on a site with good air drainage to reduce late-frost damage to early blossoms.

directions: Orangered is a California apricot cultivar notable chiefly as a breeding parent, contributing its early ripening and bright orange-red blushed skin to later California selections. Fruit is medium-sized with firm, deep orange, freestone flesh and good sweet-tart flavor, ripening early in the apricot season ahead of many standard varieties. It is not consistently self-fruitful in all plantings, so a compatible pollenizer with overlapping bloom improves yields. As with most apricots, the early bloom period leaves flowers vulnerable to a late frost, so choose a planting site with good cold-air drainage away from low spots.
sources: University of California Fruit and Nut Research and Information Center — apricot variety records
California Rare Fruit Growers — apricot cultivar notes
Dave Wilson Nursery — apricot parentage documentation

common_name: Jonamac Apple (McIntosh x Jonathan Cross, Early Northeastern Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer nearby.

directions: Jonamac was bred at Cornell University's Geneva research station from a cross of McIntosh and Jonathan and released in 1972, aiming to combine McIntosh's soft, aromatic, sweet-tart flesh with some of Jonathan's brighter tartness and slightly improved keeping quality. The medium-sized, deep red fruit ripens roughly a week to ten days ahead of standard McIntosh, giving Northeastern growers an earlier crop from a very familiar flavor profile. Like McIntosh, the flesh softens fairly quickly after harvest, so it is best used fresh or processed within a few weeks rather than stored long term. The tree is winter-hardy and productive across the cold-winter apple-growing regions of the Northeast and Upper Midwest that both parent varieties favor.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — apple breeding archives
New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva — Jonamac release records
Orange Pippin Fruit Trees — Jonamac variety notes

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after frost danger passes; the extremely compact habit makes this one of the few summer squash well suited to a large container on a patio.

directions: Patio Star is an All-America Selections winner bred for its dwarf, tidy bush habit, making it one of the only pattypan-type squash that performs well in a large pot or half-barrel rather than a garden bed. Plants stay compact and open, setting pale green to creamy-white, flying-saucer-shaped fruit that hold their tender texture and mild, buttery flavor even when a few are missed at the ideal 2-3 inch picking size. Harvest every day or two once fruiting begins, since the small plant size means missed fruit can slow overall production more noticeably than on a sprawling vine type. Feed container-grown plants regularly, since frequent watering in a pot leaches nutrients faster than in garden soil.
sources: All-America Selections award archive
Johnny's Selected Seeds catalog

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; train on a trellis for straighter fruit and better air circulation.

directions: Marketmore 70 was bred by Henry Munger at Cornell University as an early strain in the Marketmore breeding line, preceding the widely grown 1976 release Marketmore 76, which improved on it with a broader disease-resistance package. It set the vining, productive growth habit later carried forward by its successors: vigorous vines bearing straight, dark green, cylindrical slicing cucumbers with thin, non-bitter skin and crisp white flesh. Grow it on a trellis or fence where possible, since vertical training improves airflow and keeps fruit straighter and easier to pick. Harvest at 7-8 inches while still firm and uniformly dark green, checking vines daily during peak production since oversized fruit turns the plant's energy away from setting new cucumbers.
sources: Cornell University Department of Plant Breeding cucumber breeding history
USDA GRIN germplasm accession records

common_name: Perfection Pea (Heirloom Wrinkled Shelling Pea, Parent of Wando)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; like all garden peas it needs to mature before summer heat sets in.

directions: Perfection is an early-20th-century heirloom shelling pea, one of the smooth-podded, wrinkled-seeded 'marrow' dessert types once widely offered in market and home garden seed catalogs before modern hybrid peas became dominant. Sow seed directly into cool, workable spring soil, since like all garden peas it germinates and grows best well ahead of summer heat. The vigorous vines climb readily with light brush or netting support and set pods over several weeks of cool weather, yielding sweet, full-flavored peas typical of the wrinkled-seed dessert type. Perfection is historically notable as one of the two parent varieties, alongside Laxton's Progress, crossed by USDA breeders in 1943 to create the heat-tolerant Wando pea.
sources: USDA plant introduction and pea breeding records
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom pea archives

common_name: Extra Early Blackeye Cowpea (Fast-Maturing Blackeye Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed after last frost; cowpeas germinate poorly in cold ground.

directions: Extra Early Blackeye is a fast-maturing selection within the classic blackeye cowpea group, historically valued for reaching harvest noticeably sooner than standard blackeye types, an advantage for gardeners working within a short frost-free window or wanting an early flush of black-eyed peas. Direct sow seed into warm, well-drained soil after all danger of frost has passed, since cowpeas germinate poorly in cold ground. Plants carry the familiar cream-white, black-eyed seed in slender pods on compact, semi-bush vines that need little to no staking. Extra Early Blackeye has been used as breeding stock in university cowpea improvement programs, including as one of the parent lines of the disease-resistant Magnolia Blackeye released by Mississippi State University.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension Service — Southern Pea Variety Recommendations
USDA National Genetic Resources Program — cowpea germplasm records

common_name: Bunch Purple Hull Cowpea (Compact Bush-Type Purple Hull Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep into warm, lean to moderately fertile soil once the soil has thoroughly warmed after last frost.

directions: Bunch Purple Hull is a compact, upright, bush-habit selection within the purple hull class of Southern peas, bred to concentrate pods near the top of self-supporting plants rather than the sprawling growth habit of older purple hull field types. Direct sow into warm, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun once the soil has thoroughly warmed, spacing plants a few inches apart in rows. The cream-colored peas marked with a purple-pink eye retain the classic mild, slightly sweet purple hull flavor prized in Southern cooking, and pods can be picked at the green-shell stage for fresh shelling or left to dry fully for storage. Bunch Purple Hull has served as parent breeding stock for later disease-resistant purple hull and blackeye releases, including Mississippi State University's Magnolia Blackeye.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension Service — Southern Pea Variety Recommendations
USDA National Genetic Resources Program — cowpea germplasm records

common_name: Bayo Bean (Frijol Bayo, Traditional Mexican Tan Dry Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow once the soil has warmed well after last frost; like most common beans it resents cold or waterlogged ground at germination.

directions: Bayo, meaning tan or bay-colored in Spanish, is one of the principal traditional dry bean market classes of Mexico, especially common in the northern and central highland states, where its small, oval, tan seeds are a household staple distinct from the pinto, flor de mayo, and peruano classes often grown alongside it. Direct sow seed into warm soil after all frost danger has passed, since like other common beans it germinates poorly in cold, wet ground. The compact bush plants need no staking and produce a concentrated harvest well suited to home drying. Cooked bayo beans have a mild, earthy flavor and a slightly mealy, tender texture that holds together well in soups, stews, and refried preparations.
sources: Rancho Gordo
USDA Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN)

common_name: Azufrado Bean (Frijol Azufrado, Sulphur-Yellow Mexican Dry Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed; common beans germinate poorly in cold ground.

directions: Azufrado, Spanish for sulphur-colored, is a pale yellow Mexican dry bean market class especially associated with Sinaloa and other northwestern growing regions, prized for its thin skin, quick cooking time, and mild flavor that made it a major commercial bean class alongside Peruano and Flor de Mayo types. Direct sow seed into warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed, since common beans germinate poorly in cold ground. The upright bush plants require no staking and set a concentrated crop of small, oval, pale sulphur-yellow seeds that dry down uniformly for storage. Cooked azufrado beans turn a soft cream color and are valued in Mexican cooking for refried beans and soups where a smooth, quick-cooking texture is desired.
sources: Rancho Gordo
USDA Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN)
INIFAP (Instituto Nacional de Investigaciones Forestales, Agrícolas y Pecuarias, Mexico) dry bean variety releases
